newsitem.title: USA: U.S. food makers cook up home meal replacements.
newsitem.headline: U.S. food makers cook up home meal replacements.

text.p: When Amy Heber, an Internet enterpreneur and mother of two children, goes home, she faces one of the toughest decisions of her day: what to make for dinner.

"It's not a heinous task to make the family dinner, but when it's 6:30 and you're defrosting something and the kids are chirping like birds because they're hungry ...," said Heber, who owns Synasoft Inc., a Northbrook, Ill.-based company that specialises in Web sites for the Internet.

Now, the U.S. food industry is cooking up new products -- with an emphasis on fresh, not frozen foods -- to meet the demands of consumers who want to eat at home but do not have a lot of time to cook.
The concept is "home meal replacement," which has become a buzz phrase as the food industry takes another look at feeding harried professionals and two-income households with children.
It is a broad, evolving category that includes fresh, vacuum-packaged foods, expanded offerings in supermarket deli departments and ingredients for dishes that can be prepared quickly.

"Home meal replacement will run the gamut from takeout from a restaurant to going into the grocery store and getting a deli sandwich or picking up branded products (to prepare dinner quickly)," said Carol Elitov, general manager of the New Product Centre for Information Resources Inc.
In some cases, food companies are following the lead of take-out restaurants that specialise in meals consumers can eat at home.

Sara Lee Corp., for example, has launched a line of fully-prepared, fresh single-serve meals and side dishes called "Sara Lee Today's Selection," which is now marketed only in Chicago, but may later be expanded.

"We believe there are a lot of consumers who want convenient meal solutions, but also want a product that is very fresh and very high quality," said Marc Lagrois, group product manager for Bil Mar Foods Inc., a division of Sara Lee.

For some food companies, the approach to home meal replacement is made in partnership with supermarkets, who are trying to compete with take-out restaurants, according to Michael Trautschold, vice president of corporate marketing services at ConAgra Inc.
ConAgra is working with supermarket retailers to offer meals and side dishes from fully-cooked chicken breast to twice-baked potatoes.
In addition, ConAgra offers products like marinated chicken breast under its Butterball brand and frozen fish fillets under its Healthy Choice brand to help reduce meal preparation time.
"There's not one solution within a market," Trautschold said.

Kraft Foods, for example, is taking the approach that not all consumers want food that is already cooked. For Kraft, the emphasis is on "home meal components" to make a quick but satisfying dinner for a family, according to Robert Eckert, group vice president, Kraft Foods.

Kraft, which is part of Philip Morris Cos. Inc., recently launched its "Food Solution Centres," offering consumers everything in one supermarket display -- from a recipe to key ingredients -- to make a home meal.

But meal preparation time for many consumers has been trimmed to between seven and 15 minutes, from the previous average of 25 minutes, according to food industry research. At the same time, consumers say they want fresh, quality food for their families.

"It's no surprise," Elitov, of Information Resources, said of the home meal replacement trend. "More and more women are working and are more pressed for time. On the way home, they're trying to figure out what's for dinner."
